nameStory: The Arctic Surfclam gets its name from its preference for the cold northern waters of the Arctic and subarctic regions. The 'surf' part refers to where these clams are typically found - in the wave-washed sandy areas where ocean swells break along the shore. While they're called 'Arctic,' they do venture south into New England's chillier waters, especially during colder months.
description: The Arctic Surfclam is a large, robust bivalve mollusk with a thick, heavy shell that can grow quite impressive in size - sometimes reaching 4-5 inches across. Its shell has a somewhat triangular or oval shape when viewed from the side, with prominent growth rings that tell the story of its age like tree rings. The shell exterior is typically chalky white to grayish, while the interior often shows a glossy white or pale yellow surface. This is a cold-water specialist that's much less common than its southern relatives in New England waters.

idTips.label: Shell thickness and weight
idTips.description: The shell feels surprisingly heavy and thick in your hands - much more substantial than most clams you'll find on New England beaches, with walls that can be nearly half an inch thick

idTips.label: Growth rings
idTips.description: Look for very prominent, widely-spaced concentric ridges on the outside of the shell that feel rough to the touch and stand out clearly from the surface

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: The shell has a distinctly triangular or wedge-like profile when viewed from the side, rather than the rounded shape of most common clams

idTips.label: Hinge structure
idTips.description: The area where the two shell halves connect shows a large, robust triangular depression with thick, strong teeth that feel solid when you run your finger along them

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: The exterior surface has a chalky, matte finish that feels slightly rough, colored dull white to gray, often with darker staining from sediments

habitat: Arctic Surfclams are found in cold, sandy or muddy bottoms in deeper offshore waters, typically 30-300 feet deep along New England's coast. You're most likely to encounter their shells washed up on beaches after strong storms, especially on the more northern shores of Maine and New Hampshire. They prefer areas with strong currents and cold water temperatures, so they're more common during colder months or in areas influenced by cold water masses.

seasonality.spring: Empty shells may wash ashore after winter storms, often appearing bleached and worn from tumbling in cold surf. This is when you're most likely to find fresh specimens on beaches.
seasonality.summer: Living clams retreat to deeper, cooler waters offshore. Beach finds become less common as warmer surface waters prevail along the coast.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity increases the chance of finding shells washed up on beaches, especially after nor'easters bring strong onshore winds and waves.
seasonality.winter: Peak season for potential sightings as cold water temperatures bring these clams closer to shore. Shells found now are often the freshest and best preserved.

funFact: Arctic Surfclams can live for over 40 years, and scientists can read their age exactly like counting tree rings - each dark line on their shell represents one year of growth, with wider spacing during good food years and narrow rings during harsh winters.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with large Surf Clams (Spisula solidissima), but Arctic Surfclams feel noticeably heavier and thicker, with more pronounced growth ridges. Remember: 'Arctic = hefty' - if it feels surprisingly heavy for its size and has that chalky, thick shell, you've likely found the northern species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Arctic,' these clams represent the southern edge of a truly polar species' range when found in New England. Climate change is affecting their distribution, making sightings here increasingly noteworthy for tracking how northern species are responding to warming waters.
compareHints: Arctic Surfclams are the only species in their genus found in New England waters. They differ from other large clams in the trough shell family by being significantly thicker and heavier, with more prominent growth rings and a more triangular shell profile. While Surf Clams (Spisula) can get large too, they're lighter-weight with smoother shells and more rounded shapes.
